title: What stays with store staff when a robot stocks the fridge?
lead: FamilyMart has defined where people hand drink restocking over to a machine. Staff load the reserve shelf, and the robot selects bottles and places them on display. The chain measured the daily staff time saved at its early sites.

news.title: Senator's office says Jensen Huang agreed to testify in public
news.summary: An aide to US Senator Tim Scott told Reuters that former NVIDIA chief Jensen Huang had agreed to testify at a public Senate hearing. Scott's office had not given a hearing date when Reuters reported the development on November 20.
news.details: An aide to Senator Scott reported Huang's agreement to testify. The public hearing has no confirmed date.
news.technical_novelty: Lawmakers are examining the circumstances of decisions about exports of advanced computing chips to China.
news.engineering_impact: Colette Kress is acting chief executive of NVIDIA and continues to serve as chief financial officer.
news.limitations: The date originally proposed in the invitation has yet to be confirmed for the hearing.
news.evidence_status: Reuters attributes the development to the senator's office. NVIDIA's board announcement and earnings report separately establish the leadership transition.
news.body:
Former NVIDIA chief Jensen Huang has agreed to testify at a public US Senate hearing, an aide to Senator Tim Scott told Reuters on November 20. Lawmakers are asking about exports of advanced computing chips to China. For organizations that use such chips to train models, what the former executive can explain and who speaks for the supplier today are separate practical questions.

Scott, who chairs the Senate Banking Committee, had invited Huang to appear before the panel. ABC News earlier reported on the letters to Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick. Senators are examining circumstances that may have influenced decisions on exports to China of advanced chips used for artificial intelligence. The substance of Huang's answers will become available if the hearing takes place. A spokesperson for Huang declined to comment to Reuters about the hearing.

Buyers of computing equipment also have reason to pay attention to the capacity in which Huang would appear. On November 12 NVIDIA's board announced his immediate resignation as president, chief executive and a board member. Chief financial officer Colette Kress became interim chief executive. The company's November 17 earnings announcement continued to identify her in both roles. Customers seeking a current product or supply commitment therefore have a different point of authority from the witness being called to discuss past decisions.

Scott's initial request mentioned December 3, but his office did not confirm a date when reporting Huang's agreement. A separate closed interview with House committees was scheduled for December 1. The two proceedings offer different opportunities for the public to hear the answers.

news.title: What FamilyMart measured before expanding automated drink restocking
news.summary: Japan's FamilyMart will begin a phased rollout of Telexistence drink-stocking robots in January 2027. Staff load a digital storage shelf, while sales at the individual shop help determine which drinks the robot puts on display first.
news.details: A worker loads the reserve drinks first. The robot moves bottles onto the shelf facing the shoppers.
news.technical_novelty: The system tracks the location of the drinks and uses the shop's sales history.
news.engineering_impact: A drink that sells quickly can get priority when the machine restocks the display.
news.limitations: The roughly 70 percent saving refers to staff time spent restocking drinks per day at the early stores.
news.evidence_status: FamilyMart and Telexistence described the early stores and the phased rollout planned from January 2027.
news.body:
FamilyMart plans to start handing drink display work to robots in more Japanese shops in January 2027. At its early sites the chain measured a reduction of about 70 percent in daily staff time spent replenishing drinks. A shop adopting the system needs both the machine that transfers bottles and the storage shelf that keeps track of them.

Staff used to handle the same delivery at two points in its journey. They sorted the incoming drinks inside the fridge, then checked what customers had taken and carried bottles from storage to the display. In the new arrangement, the storage shelf marks the handover. A worker scans the first bottle and puts the stock away. The shelf keeps track of product locations and quantities, even when different items share the storage space. It can also suggest how many bottles of each item are needed.

A separate machine takes care of the display. Its control system uses the store's sales history to give popular products priority. The retailer and its technology partner have been working together on the equipment since 2020. FamilyMart quotes a maximum of about 1,800 bottles stocked per day. That figure describes the machine's capacity. To assess the effect on staff, the chain tracked time spent replenishing drinks per store per day.

A franchise operator can put the percentage to work by measuring how much time the existing shifts actually spend replenishing drinks. That provides the baseline for a staffing calculation. Receiving the delivery and loading the reserve shelf both remain part of the store team's work.

news.title: Green Logistics uses six robots to stack cases leaving storage
news.summary: Mujin described six robots working at a new Green Logistics warehouse in Japan. They receive cases from automated storage, locate them and stack them on pallets for shipment.
news.details: At the new Green Logistics centre, six machines receive cases from automated storage.
news.technical_novelty: A camera on the arm measures depth. Software works out where to place the case.
news.engineering_impact: The camera needs no separate stand beside the robot, which helps the equipment fit the available floor space.
news.limitations: Around 500 cases an hour is the rate given for one machine at this site.
news.evidence_status: Mujin, the supplier, described the installation and its rate in a report published on November 19.
news.body:
Green Logistics has put robots to work between storage and dispatch at its new Japanese logistics centre. The supplier, Mujin, published an account of the operating installation on November 19. It reports six machines on site and a handling rate of roughly five hundred cases an hour per machine.

Cases arrive individually from storage. The machines have to stack them on a pallet, a flat base on which several cases can travel together as one load. For an arm, each placement changes the space available for the next case. The MujinOS software chooses a stacking position while the system is working. It uses a view with depth from a camera on the arm to recognize and locate the case in front of it. The supplier says the equipment handles roughly a thousand kinds of cases.

Floor space also shaped the installation. The six work cells sit directly beside the automated storage system, packed into a limited area. Putting the camera on the arm dispenses with a separate stand alongside each robot. The system takes possible collisions into account as it plans the movement. Mujin reports a rate of about five hundred cases picked and stacked per hour for an individual machine at the site.

A buyer estimating site capacity would also need to know how regularly storage feeds the cells and how quickly finished pallets leave. The per-cell figure helps size the incoming flow. The account gives no full-shift shipment total from which to establish how long the whole building sustains that pace.

news.title: Japanese partners test the handover from a parcel locker to a delivery robot
news.summary: Fulltime System and NEC Magnus Communications began joint testing on November 17 of a delivery system for apartment buildings. They will examine how a box leaves a shared locker, travels between floors and is set down safely outside a resident's door.
news.details: The robot is intended to collect the parcel downstairs, take the lift and leave the box outside an apartment.
news.technical_novelty: The partners are improving the mechanism that transfers the parcel from a locker to the robot.
news.engineering_impact: Delivery between floors requires the robot and the lift to work together.
news.limitations: The companies announced the start of testing. They have yet to give a completed delivery rate.
news.evidence_status: Fulltime System and NEC Magnus Communications set out the aims of their joint trial starting November 17.
news.organization: Fulltime System and NEC Magnus Communications
news.body:
Two Japanese partners have begun testing whether a robot can take over the final stretch of a delivery inside a residential building. Fulltime System and NEC Magnus Communications launched a joint trial on November 17 linking the parcel locker, lift and unloading point at the door. For a building manager, those are three distinct places where equipment has to work together.

In the proposed service, a courier takes a parcel to a shared locker at the entrance. A resident who opts into the service would receive the box at the apartment door. In between, the machine takes the parcel from its compartment, calls the lift, boards it, gets out on the right floor and travels along the corridor. After unloading it returns to a waiting point. Following a single order through the service therefore means observing several handovers, including the transfer from a stationary locker to a mobile platform.

Fulltime System previously tested delivery linked to a lift at its Fukuoka branch in November 2023. The partners now plan to improve the parcel retrieval mechanism together. NEC Magnus Communications will develop the robot and its controls and test how practically and safely it can leave a parcel at the door. The partners will jointly assess operation and durability under conditions close to those in an apartment building.

A property manager considering the service would need details of compatibility with the building's lifts and of what happens to a parcel if a handover is interrupted. The announcement sets out what the trial will examine. It gives neither a completed deliveries figure per shift nor a cost per trip.

news.title: What the wearable tools cost for recording a towel fold away from the robot
news.summary: Brik Meza and colleagues presented HandUMI, a pair of wearable devices that record a person's movements without using a robot. One controller trained on 562 demonstrations completed a towel fold in 12 of 20 attempts on a physical pair of arms.
news.details: A person folded a towel using two tools worn on the hands. The recordings were used to train programs for real robot arms.
news.technical_novelty: Sensors recorded each hand's path and the gap between the parts that gripped the cloth.
news.engineering_impact: People could collect examples away from the robot that would later attempt the fold.
news.limitations: After training on 562 demonstrations, one program completed 12 of 20 folds and the other completed seven of 20.
news.evidence_status: Brik Meza and colleagues described their test on physical robot arms in a paper posted November 17.
news.body:
Brik Meza and colleagues have shown a way to collect training examples without occupying a pair of robot arms for every demonstration. In their HandUMI project, people folded towels with wearable tools. The researchers needed the physical arms later, when the resulting controller had to work with real cloth. Both the hardware design and the software are open source.

The demonstrator wears a tool on each hand with parallel jaws that slide together and apart. Swappable tips match the shape of the parts that will touch the object on the intended robot. Virtual reality controllers track the hands, while a separate sensor measures the gap between the jaws. This records both the path of a tool and when it closes or opens on the cloth. For another robot, software calculates how its joints would have to move to take its gripper along the recorded path.

The authors tested that calculation on seven simulated arm configurations. A separate physical experiment used a pair of PiPER arms to fold a towel. With the full set of 562 demonstrations, one controller, ACT, completed 12 of 20 attempts. A second, a fine-tuned model called π0.5, completed seven of twenty. Training ACT on only the first 101 demonstrations produced no completed folds in twenty attempts.

The authors price a pair of recording devices with Quest 3S tracking at 557 US dollars, excluding the host computer and optional ZED Mini camera. That gives a procurement starting point for recording equipment. A trial budget would also have to cover access to the arms and the operator time needed to demonstrate and evaluate the selected task.

technology_signal.title: FamilyMart measured restocking time before expanding its rollout
technology_signal.summary: FamilyMart reports that daily staff time spent replenishing drinks fell by about 70 percent in early stores. From January 2027 it plans to introduce the robots in stages together with digital storage shelves.
technology_signal.implications: To estimate the effect at an individual shop, an operator needs its baseline staff time spent restocking drinks. Receiving deliveries and loading the reserve shelf remain part of the staff workload.
